terms: what is snap called in the virgin islands
supplements.citation: USVI DHS Family Assistance Programs page (dhs.vi.gov/family-assistance-programs/); USDA FNS/FNA Virgin Islands SNAP directory entry
supplements.heading: USVI's SNAP is administered centrally by DHS's Division of Family Assistance across three district offices (St. Croix, St. Thomas, St. John) — and, distinctively among this roster's packs, there is NO online self-service application portal
supplements.text: The U.S. Virgin Islands Department of Human Services (DHS), through its Division of Family Assistance (DFA), administers SNAP directly for the territory — a single, centrally administered program with three physical district offices: St. Croix (STX), St. Thomas (STT), and St. John (STJ), each with its own phone extension. DHS's own consumer materials give SNAP's EBT card a distinctive local nickname: the 'sun, sand & sea' card. This pack found a genuine structural difference from every other pack in this roster so far: USVI DHS's own Family Assistance Programs page describes NO online self-service application portal — no equivalent of Delaware's ASSIST, California's BenefitsCal, or any other state's web-based apply flow. Instead, an applicant must complete a paper 'Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and CASH Assistance Combined Application,' obtained by picking it up at a local SNAP office, having one mailed by calling the local office, or printing it from DHS's own website — then submit it in person, by mail, by email, by fax, or via a district-office drop box. This pack treats the absence of an online portal as a disclosed, genuine access-model finding, not a research gap: DHS-VI's own page lists these specific submission channels and names no digital-submission alternative. If you qualify, DHS states you should receive benefits within 30 days of application receipt, or 7 days for expedited cases. The Division of Family Assistance's listed program administrator is Natalie Bailey.

supplements.citation: USDA FNS/FNA Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility policy page (current); USVI DHS FY2026 SNAP Monthly Allotments and Deductions table; vi.gov official press release (10/2024)
supplements.heading: CONFIRMATION (not merely a secondary-source claim): USVI's BBCE gross-income gate is 175% of the federal poverty guideline, with NO resource/asset limit for any household — confirmed directly on USDA's own current official BBCE page
supplements.text: This pack found a claim repeated across several secondary/aggregator sources (that the Virgin Islands has 'no asset limit' under a 175% FPL BBCE gate) and specifically chased it to USDA's own current, live Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility policy page rather than accepting the aggregator framing at face value — and found it independently confirmed there in USDA's own words: the Virgin Islands is listed with 'All households' categorically eligible (the broadest BBCE implementation tier, alongside states like Delaware, New Hampshire, and Maryland), 'No limit on assets,' and a gross income limit of '175%' of the federal poverty guideline. This is corroborated by a second source: a Food Research & Action Center (FRAC) compilation explicitly sourced from the same USDA BBCE page. A vi.gov official press release, quoting DHS Commissioner Averil George directly, confirms the underlying policy change and its effective date: the gross-income threshold rose from 130% to 175% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines effective October 1, 2024 — meaning 175% is a genuinely recent USVI-specific policy choice, not a static federal default. This pack flags one internal ambiguity it could NOT fully resolve: DHS-VI's own FY2026 Monthly Allotments and Deductions table displays BOTH a '175% of Poverty' column and, immediately adjacent, a '200% of Poverty' column, with no explanatory text distinguishing which households the 200% figure applies to. This pack treats USDA's own official BBCE page — which states a single, unambiguous 175% figure with no bifurcation — as authoritative for the applicable categorical-eligibility income gate, and discloses the DHS-VI table's second, unexplained column as an unresolved internal ambiguity rather than guessing at its meaning; see freshness.json.

supplements.citation: USDA FNS/FNA SNAP State Options Report, 17th Edition (Dec 2025, data as of 10/1/2024) — Virgin Islands state page
supplements.heading: CONFIRMATION: USVI has FULLY opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP disqualification
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state (or territory) opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). This pack found the answer directly on USDA's own most current State Options Report (17th edition, published December 2025, using FFY2025 State Plan data as of October 1, 2024): the Virgin Islands' 'Drug Felony Disqualifications' policy option is listed plainly as 'No disqualification' — the fullest possible opt-out tier, the same category this roster's Delaware, North Dakota, and several other packs independently confirmed for their own jurisdictions. This pack did not locate a USVI-specific statute or regulation citation (e.g., a numbered Virgin Islands Code section) establishing this opt-out — DHS-VI's own public-facing materials do not appear to cite the specific enabling law, and this pack did not find a codified USVI SNAP policy manual publicly posted (unlike, e.g., Delaware's numbered DSSM sections). This pack treats USDA's own State Options Report as authoritative for the POLICY OUTCOME (no drug-felony disqualification applies) while disclosing that the underlying USVI-specific statutory citation remains unlocated — see freshness.json.

supplements.citation: USVI DHS SNAP Work Requirements/ABAWD webpage PDF and 'SNAP Benefits Are Changing' flyer (current, 2026); USDA FNS/FNA SNAP State Options Report, 17th Edition (Dec 2025, 10/1/2024 data)
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL/TIMING FINDING: USVI's post-OBBBA ABAWD work requirement takes effect March 1, 2026 — roughly four months AFTER the mainland's November 1, 2025 OBBBA effective date this roster's other packs confirm; as of the most recent published federal data USVI still had a statewide ABAWD waiver on file
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is normally limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 3-year period absent a qualifying work activity or an exemption. USVI DHS's own current (2026-dated) ABAWD webpage PDF and 'SNAP Benefits Are Changing' flyer state that, following the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, signed July 4, 2025), new ABAWD work rules take effect in the Virgin Islands starting March 1, 2026, with the current three-year time-limit window running March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2029. This pack flags this as a genuine, USVI-specific implementation-timing difference worth disclosing explicitly: this roster's mainland packs (e.g., Delaware) confirm the OBBBA ABAWD changes took effect nationally on November 1, 2025 — USVI's own materials describe a later, territory-specific March 1, 2026 start date, roughly four months after the mainland date. This pack did not find an explicit USDA or DHS-VI statement of WHY the date differs (e.g., a formal territory-specific phase-in provision versus USVI's own prior waiver simply running its course) and discloses this as an open question rather than guessing at causation. Separately, this pack notes that USDA's own 17th-edition State Options Report (published Dec 2025, but using data as of 10/1/2024, i.e., PRE-OBBBA) lists USVI's 'ABAWD Time Limit Waiver' status as 'Statewide ABAWD time limit waiver' — a snapshot from before OBBBA's own changes to state/territory waiver eligibility took effect, and NOT evidence of a currently active waiver under the new post-3/1/2026 regime. The current, applicable rules per DHS-VI's own materials: the ABAWD requirement applies to ages 18-64 (post-OBBBA, up from the pre-OBBBA ceiling), without a child under 14 in the household, and considered able to work at least 20 hours/week; the exemption list includes being exempt from general work registration (except when solely for being 18-59), under 18 or 65+, living with a child under 14, pregnant, being 'An Indian,' 'Urban Indian,' or 'California Indian,' or a certified physical/mental barrier to employment lasting 30+ days. General work registration (distinct from the ABAWD time limit) applies to ages 16-59 with its own exemption list (caring for a child under 6 or incapacitated person, working 30+ hrs/week or earning $217.50+/week, unemployment benefits, disability benefits, physically/mentally unfit, half-time school/training, JOBS program compliance, drug/alcohol treatment program).

supplements.citation: USVI DHS FY2026 SNAP Monthly Allotments and Deductions table (10/1/2025-9/30/2026); USDA FNS/FNA SNAP State Options Report, 17th Edition (Dec 2025, 10/1/2024 data)
supplements.heading: USVI's own FY2026 table hardcodes specific dollar figures for its standard deduction, shelter deduction cap, telephone deduction, and homeless-shelter deduction — but the federal State Options Report separately lists USVI's Standard Utility Allowance as 'not mandatory,' an apparent internal tension this pack discloses rather than resolves
supplements.text: USVI DHS's own current FY2026 (October 1, 2025 - September 30, 2026) Monthly Allotments and Deductions table gives specific, hardcoded dollar figures: a Standard Deduction that varies by household size ($184 for 1-2 person households, $185 for 3, $223 for 4, $261 for 5, $299 for 6+), a Maximum Shelter Deduction of $586.00, a Telephone Deduction of $34.00, a Homeless Shelter Deduction of $198.99 (matching the current federal FY2026 maximum this roster's other packs also confirm), and a Minimum Allotment of $31 for 1-2 person households (the standard national minimum allotment figure). This pack separately found, in USDA's own 17th-edition State Options Report, that the Virgin Islands' 'Treatment of Utility Expenses' policy option is listed as 'SUAs not mandatory' — meaning USVI is not required to use a flat Standard Utility Allowance (SUA) methodology the way most mainland states do, and may instead calculate actual utility costs per household in at least some cases. This pack could not fully reconcile these two facts: DHS-VI's own table presents a flat $586.00 shelter-deduction cap and $34.00 telephone-deduction figure as if they function like standard allowances, while the federal report says SUAs are not mandatory for USVI. This pack discloses the apparent tension rather than resolving it with false confidence — an applicant or caseworker should confirm directly with DHS-VI's DFA whether their specific shelter/utility costs are calculated via these table figures or via actual documented costs.

supplements.citation: USDA FNS/FNA SNAP Restaurant Meals Program page (current, live list of participating states)
supplements.heading: USVI does NOT operate a Restaurant Meals Program
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state/territory OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT. This pack fetched USDA's own current, live RMP page directly and confirmed the published list of participating jurisdictions (Arizona, California, Illinois — Cook and Franklin Counties only, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Rhode Island, and others) does NOT include the Virgin Islands. This pack found no USVI DHS page or press release describing a pending or planned RMP. This pack's reading: the operative answer for a USVI applicant asking whether they can use SNAP at a restaurant is currently no — this is a direct confirmation from USDA's own current published list, not an absence-of-evidence inference from silence alone.

supplements.citation: USDA FNS/FNA SNAP State Options Report, 17th Edition (Dec 2025, 10/1/2024 data); USVI DHS FY2026 Simplified Reporting Requirements
supplements.heading: USVI puts ALL SNAP households on simplified reporting, with certification periods that can run 6, 12, or 24 months depending on circumstance — this pack could not locate which specific household types get which length
supplements.text: USDA's own 17th-edition State Options Report confirms USVI's 'Reporting Requirements' policy is 'Simplified reporting only' (no household is on full change-reporting) and its 'Certification Period Lengths' option includes all three of 6 months, 12 months, and 24 months. USVI DHS's own FY2026 Simplified Reporting Requirements document independently confirms the simplified-reporting structure directly: 'All SNAP HOUSEHOLDS ARE ON SIMPLIFIED REPORTING,' with a household must report an income increase only if it pushes gross monthly income above the 130% federal-poverty-guideline threshold shown in a household-size table (e.g., $1,696/month for a household of 1, $3,483/month for a household of 4), reported within 10 days after the end of the month it occurred. The only OTHER mandatory-report event is a single lottery/gambling winning of $4,500 or more; all other changes are optional to report (though DHS encourages reporting changes that could increase benefits). Cash Assistance households face a stricter standard: they must report ALL changes by the 10th day of the following month. This pack flags a genuine, disclosed gap: unlike this roster's Delaware pack (which found DSSM 9068's own text specifying which household types get the 12-month vs. 24-month tier), this pack could not locate a USVI-specific breakdown explaining which household circumstances receive the 6-month vs. 12-month vs. 24-month certification length — the State Options Report confirms all three lengths are used as options, but not the assignment rule. Do not assume any one length without confirming with DHS-VI's DFA directly.

supplements.citation: USVI DHS Family Assistance Programs page; 7 CFR 273.10 (federal benefit calculation, applies identically in USVI as federal floor)
supplements.heading: USVI applies the standard federal citizenship/immigration eligibility rule (citizens, qualified non-citizens, 5-year waiting period) and the standard federal net-income-to-benefit calculation — this territory has NOT modified either
supplements.text: DHS-VI's own Family Assistance Programs page states the applicant eligibility rule directly: 'Citizens and qualified alien non-citizens who legally live in the U.S. or U.S. Territories' may apply, with a standard 5-year waiting period for most non-citizens (though DHS's own text notes 'anyone can apply' — meaning the waiting period is assessed at eligibility determination, not at the application-submission stage), and Social Security numbers must be provided for everyone in the household. This pack found no USVI-specific deviation from the federal noncitizen eligibility framework in any source it fetched, unlike, e.g., Delaware's disclosed 4/1/2026 noncitizen-eligibility-narrowing change; this pack did not specifically verify whether that same federal change applies identically and on the same date in USVI, and flags this as an unconfirmed extension rather than assuming parity, see freshness.json. This pack also found no USVI-specific override of the standard federal SNAP benefit-calculation formula (7 CFR 273.10) — USVI's own FY2026 table applies the federal formula (net income subtracted from the federal Thrifty Food Plan maximum allotment for the household's size, using the standard/earned-income/dependent-care/medical/excess-shelter deductions this pack confirmed) with USVI's own COLA-adjusted dollar inputs, the same federal-floor mechanism this roster's other packs confirm rather than a distinctive USVI-specific benefit formula.

terms: does the virgin islands run snap
supplements.citation: USDA FNS/FNA Virgin Islands SNAP directory entry; USDA FNS/FNA SNAP State Options Report, 17th Edition (Dec 2025, 10/1/2024 data)
supplements.heading: CONFIRMATION: the U.S. Virgin Islands runs standard federal SNAP directly — NOT the Nutrition Assistance Program (NAP) block grant that Puerto Rico, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands run instead
supplements.text: Three U.S. territories — Puerto Rico, American Samoa, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands — do NOT run SNAP; they run the Nutrition Assistance Program (NAP), a federal block grant under which the territory itself sets eligibility rules and benefit levels, rather than following the SNAP rules this corpus otherwise describes. This pack independently re-verified, rather than assumed, that the U.S. Virgin Islands is NOT one of those three territories: USDA's own SNAP state directory entry names the Virgin Islands' program plainly as 'Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP),' and USDA's own 17th-edition State Options Report (Dec 2025) states in its own introduction that 'SNAP State agencies include all 50 States, the District of Columbia, Guam, and the Virgin Islands' — devoting a full state-summary page to the Virgin Islands' own SNAP policy options, the same treatment given to every state, and NOT given to Puerto Rico, American Samoa, or CNMI. This pack's conclusion: an applicant in the U.S. Virgin Islands is applying for the same federal SNAP program (with USVI's own BBCE/deduction/reporting policy choices layered on top, as this pack's other supplements describe), not a separate territory-specific block grant.
